cur:objects-monasterboice-west-cross.summary: This very tall, slender cross stands beside the ruined church at Monasterboice; its west face is divided into panels of scriptural scenes, with the Crucifixion at the centre of the ringed head. Christ is shown on the cross with arms outstretched, in the tradition of the Irish high crosses that place the saving death of Christ at the very heart of the cross. Weathering has softened the carving, but the whole programme still leads the eye upward to the crucified Lord.
facts: Monasterboice has three high crosses, the North, West and South (Muiredach's) crosses; Wikipedia notes that the North and West crosses have suffered much more from weathering than Muiredach's Cross.
On Irish 'scripture' crosses the west face usually carries New Testament scenes, with the Crucifixion in the centre of the head (type).
cur:objects-monasterboice-west-cross.notes: The Crucifixion is small in this full view of the cross.

feat:lorsch-gospels-ivory-christ-treadin.summary: At the centre of this five-part ivory cover, a youthful Christ holding a long cross and the Gospel book tramples the lion, the asp, the dragon and the basilisk, flanked by two archangels; above, angels carry a medallion of the cross, and smaller scenes fill the panel below. The design consciously imitates sixth-century imperial ivories, translating Byzantine and late Roman models into a Carolingian proclamation of Christ's victory over evil. It once protected one of the most sumptuous Gospel books of Charlemagne's age.
facts: The Lorsch Gospels were later split: the Gospels of Matthew and Mark are in Alba Iulia, Romania, while Luke and John are in the Vatican Library and this back cover is in the Vatican's Museo Sacro; the front cover, with the Virgin and Child, is in the Victoria and Albert Museum, London.
The image of Christ trampling beasts illustrates Psalm 91 (90), a theme also found in a Ravenna mosaic of Christ as warrior earlier in this journey.
The five-part format, with a large central panel surrounded by four smaller ones, revives the structure of late antique imperial diptychs such as the Barberini Ivory.
The manuscript takes its name from the Abbey of Lorsch, in Germany, where it was kept in the Middle Ages.
